HCC pilot — random-effect vs interaction tissue formula

V1_nk liver baseline sanity check on 4 TIMES biomarkers

Author
Affiliation

Chen Zhan

SAiGENCI, The University of Adelaide

Published

15 Jul 2026

Abstract

Pilot comparison of two posteriorHCA V1_nk brms parameterisations for the comprehensive healthy liver NK baseline used in the TIMES HCC case study: a random-effect formula that treats tissue-specific covariate slopes as random effects, and a fixed interaction alternative where covariates interact with tissue_groups. This revision refits BOTH families on the login node with a simplified shape (dispersion) formula — dropping the ethnicity/tissue-specific shape terms so the shape can borrow power across tissues rather than being limited by small per-tissue samples (liver n = 71) — and, for each family, also refits the previous rich shape as a reference. We test the hypothesis that the shape formula, not the mean formula, drives the large posterior SD of the liver baseline, then project the four TIMES HCC cohorts (IF/TC x REC/non-REC) onto the revised baselines and ask which formula best serves the case study by preserving the expected ordering that recurrent cohorts sit farther from healthy than non-recurrent cohorts.

Motivation

The TIMES HCC case study uses a comprehensive healthy liver NK baseline from the posteriorHCA V1_nk atlas. Each gene is modelled as a zero-inflated negative binomial regression on pseudobulk counts with rich covariate structure. In production, tissue-specific deviations enter as random effects:

\[ \texttt{(1 + age\_decade * sex + ethnicity\_groups | tissue\_groups)} \]

This partial pooling is attractive when many tissues contribute information, but liver contributes only 71 of 3,226 NK pseudobulk samples (2.2%), while blood contributes 74%. A concern for the HCC application is that liver tissue effects — and liver-specific age/sex/ethnicity slopes — may be shrunk toward the blood-dominated population mean, appearing as if liver biology is embedded in the global fixed effect rather than estimated independently.

An alternative is to replace the random-slopes tissue term with fixed interactions:

\[ \texttt{age\_decade:tissue\_groups + sex:tissue\_groups + ...} \]

This removes hierarchical shrinkage: liver coefficients are estimated only from liver rows. The trade-off is a much larger parameter space and potential instability when liver sample size is modest.

The shape (dispersion) formula, revisited

Both families share the same negative-binomial shape (dispersion) sub-model. In the previous pilot the shape formula carried tissue- and ethnicity-specific terms, so the liver dispersion was estimated largely from the 71 liver rows. We hypothesise that this shape structure — not the mean formula — is what inflates the posterior SD of the liver baseline: a poorly identified per-tissue dispersion widens the joint posterior, including the mean linear predictor log(μ) we read off as the baseline.

This revision therefore simplifies the shape formula so dispersion borrows power across all tissues instead of being anchored to small per-tissue samples:

  • Interaction shape → shape ~ 1 + disease_groups_altered + assay_groups_altered
  • Random-effect shape → shape ~ 1 + disease_groups_altered + assay_groups_altered + (1 | tissue_groups)

To attribute any SD change to the shape formula rather than the mean formula, we refit each family under both the revised simple shape and the previous rich shape while holding the counts formula fixed.

This report is a pilot on four TIMES biomarkers present in the V1_nk store. It compares both families (random-effect and interaction) x both shape variants (simple and rich). The fits are precomputed once by R/HCC_re_vs_interaction_pilot.R (run on a compute node with cores = 32; the random-slopes RE fit is too heavy for the login node) and cached as fit_<family>[_rich]_<GENE>.rds under params$out_dir. The training data and the rich-shape RE reference are read from the production targets store. Rendering only reads the cached artefacts — it never fits models.

Formulas compared

Each family keeps its own counts (mean) formula and is fit under two shape (dispersion) formulas: the revised simple shape and the previous rich shape. The counts formula is identical across the two shape variants, so any difference in the baseline is attributable to the shape sub-model alone.

Code 
source(file.path(params$case_dir, "R", "re_vs_interaction_helpers.R"))
specs <- formula_specs()

knitr::kable(data.frame(
  family = c("random-effect", "random-effect", "random-effect",
             "interaction", "interaction", "interaction"),
  component = c("counts", "shape (rich, reference)", "shape (simple, revised)",
                "counts", "shape (rich, reference)", "shape (simple, revised)"),
  formula = c(specs$re$counts, specs$re$shape_rich, specs$re$shape_simple,
              specs$interaction$counts, specs$interaction$shape_rich, specs$interaction$shape_simple)
))
family component formula
random-effect counts counts ~ 1 + offset(offset) + age_decade * sex + disease_groups_altered + ethnicity_groups + assay_groups_altered + (1 | dataset_id_altered) + (1 + age_decade * sex + ethnicity_groups | tissue_groups)
random-effect shape (rich, reference) shape ~ 1 + disease_groups_altered + assay_groups_altered + ethnicity_groups + (1 | tissue_groups)
random-effect shape (simple, revised) shape ~ 1 + disease_groups_altered + assay_groups_altered + (1 | tissue_groups)
interaction counts counts ~ 1 + offset(offset) + disease_groups_altered + assay_groups_altered + (1 | dataset_id_altered) + tissue_groups + age_decade:tissue_groups + sex:tissue_groups + age_decade:sex:tissue_groups + ethnicity_groups:tissue_groups
interaction shape (rich, reference) shape ~ 1 + disease_groups_altered + assay_groups_altered + ethnicity_groups + tissue_groups
interaction shape (simple, revised) shape ~ 1 + disease_groups_altered + assay_groups_altered

The random-effect counts formula treats tissue deviations as random slopes; the interaction counts formula is their fixed-effect expansion inside tissue_groups. The rich shape carries ethnicity_groups (and a tissue term), while the simple shape drops those so dispersion pools across tissues.

Load precomputed baselines (fits are NOT run during rendering)

For each gene we fit four brms models — {random-effect, interaction} x {simple, rich shape} — with cores = 32. The random-slopes RE fit is expensive and must run on a compute node, not the login node and not during rendering. Fits are therefore precomputed once by R/HCC_re_vs_interaction_pilot.R and cached as fit_re_<GENE>.rds, fit_interaction_<GENE>.rds (revised simple shape) and fit_interaction_rich_<GENE>.rds (reference); the rich-shape RE reference reuses the production store fit. This chunk only reads the cached artefacts, so the report renders in seconds.

To (re)generate the cache before rendering (on an allocated compute node):

module load R/4.5.3-gfbf-2025b
REFRESH_FITS=true Rscript R/HCC_re_vs_interaction_pilot.R
Code 
model_labels <- c(re = "Random effect", interaction = "Interaction")
shape_labels <- c(simple = "Simple shape (revised)", rich = "Rich shape (reference)")

comparison_csv <- file.path(params$out_dir, "baseline_comparison_by_formula.csv")
shape_effect_csv <- file.path(params$out_dir, "baseline_shape_effect.csv")
draws_csv <- file.path(params$out_dir, "baseline_draws_long.csv")

if (!all(file.exists(comparison_csv, shape_effect_csv, draws_csv))) {
  stop(
    "Precomputed pilot artefacts not found in params$out_dir.\n",
    "Rendering does NOT fit models (the random-slopes RE fit must run on a ",
    "compute node). Run the batch fitter first, e.g.:\n",
    "  module load R/4.5.3-gfbf-2025b\n",
    "  REFRESH_FITS=true Rscript ",
    file.path(params$case_dir, "R", "HCC_re_vs_interaction_pilot.R"), "\n",
    "then re-render."
  )
}

baseline_summary <- read_csv(comparison_csv, show_col_types = FALSE)
shape_effect <- read_csv(shape_effect_csv, show_col_types = FALSE)
draws_df <- read_csv(draws_csv, show_col_types = FALSE)

draws_labelled <- draws_df |>
  mutate(
    model_label = recode(model, !!!model_labels),
    shape_label = recode(shape_variant, !!!shape_labels),
    model_label = factor(model_label, levels = c("Random effect", "Interaction")),
    shape_label = factor(shape_label, levels = shape_labels)
  )

Comprehensive liver baseline comparison

For each gene x family x shape we compute the same comprehensive healthy liver baseline used in the universal HCC case study:

  • disease_groups_altered = Normal
  • tissue_groups = liver
  • offset = 0
  • marginalised over the full atlas grid of sex × age_decade × ethnicity × assay
  • posterior_linpred(transform = FALSE) then averaged across grid rows per draw
Code 
baseline_summary |>
  mutate(
    model = recode(model, !!!model_labels),
    shape = recode(shape_variant, !!!shape_labels),
    across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3))
  ) |>
  select(
    gene, model, shape, fit_source,
    mean_log_mu, sd_log_mu, median_mu, max_rhat, n_liver_rows
  ) |>
  arrange(gene, model, shape)

Does the shape formula control the baseline SD?

The central question: within each family (holding the counts formula fixed), does the simple shape shrink the posterior SD of the liver baseline relative to the rich shape? sd_ratio_simple_over_rich < 1 and a positive sd_reduction support the hypothesis.

Code 
shape_effect |>
  mutate(
    model = recode(model, !!!model_labels),
    across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3))
  ) |>
  select(
    gene, model,
    sd_log_mu_rich, sd_log_mu_simple, sd_ratio_simple_over_rich, sd_reduction,
    mean_log_mu_rich, mean_log_mu_simple, mean_shift_simple_minus_rich
  ) |>
  arrange(model, gene)
Code 
baseline_summary |>
  mutate(
    model_label = factor(recode(model, !!!model_labels),
                         levels = c("Random effect", "Interaction")),
    shape_label = factor(recode(shape_variant, !!!shape_labels),
                         levels = shape_labels)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = gene, y = sd_log_mu, fill = shape_label)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.7), width = 0.65) +
  facet_wrap(~ model_label) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    `Rich shape (reference)` = "#E64B35",
    `Simple shape (revised)` = "#4DBBD5"
  )) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Posterior SD of comprehensive liver log(mu)",
    fill = NULL,
    title = "Baseline uncertainty by shape formula",
    subtitle = "Lower simple-shape bars would confirm the shape controls the SD"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

The overlaid posterior densities make the narrowing (or not) directly visible: each panel is a gene, colour is the family, and line type distinguishes the two shape formulas.

Code 
n_narrower <- sum(shape_effect$sd_ratio_simple_over_rich < 1, na.rm = TRUE)
n_total <- sum(is.finite(shape_effect$sd_ratio_simple_over_rich))
mean_ratio <- mean(shape_effect$sd_ratio_simple_over_rich, na.rm = TRUE)

cat(glue(
  "The simple shape yields a narrower baseline in **{n_narrower}/{n_total}** ",
  "gene x family cells, with a mean SD ratio (simple / rich) of ",
  "**{round(mean_ratio, 2)}**. ",
  if (n_narrower > n_total / 2) {
    "This supports the hypothesis that the shape formula — not the mean formula — is the dominant driver of the liver baseline SD: pooling dispersion across tissues tightens the posterior."
  } else {
    "This does not support a dominant shape-formula effect on the baseline SD; the mean formula and sample size likely dominate."
  }
))

The simple shape yields a narrower baseline in 3/8 gene x family cells, with a mean SD ratio (simple / rich) of 0.99. This does not support a dominant shape-formula effect on the baseline SD; the mean formula and sample size likely dominate.

HCC cohort projection onto both baselines

The point of the baseline is to serve the TIMES HCC case study. We therefore project the four HCC cohorts (IF/TC x REC/non-REC) onto both baseline formulas and ask which one better matches the case-study expectation. Cohort log(μ) values are the edgeR NB estimates at offset = 0 produced by the universal-baseline report and are independent of the atlas formula, so the same cohort projections can be overlaid on either baseline density.

Code 
cohort_tests <- read_csv(params$cohort_results_csv, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  select(gene, cohort, compartment, recurrence, cohort_log_mu, cohort_se) |>
  filter(gene %in% unique(draws_df$gene))

Baseline densities per gene, with HCC cohorts

For each gene we plot the posterior log(μ) density of both revised (simple-shape) baselines (random-effect vs interaction) and overlay the four HCC cohort projections as vertical lines — the direct analogue of the universal case-study figure, split by model family.

Code 
model_colours <- c(`Random effect` = "#4DBBD5", Interaction = "#E64B35")
cohort_colours <- c(
  IF_REC = "#C23B4A",
  IF_non_REC = "#2878B5",
  TC_REC = "#E08A2E",
  TC_non_REC = "#2D8B57"
)

draws_plot <- draws_df |>
  filter(shape_variant == "simple") |>
  mutate(
    model = recode(model, !!!model_labels),
    model = factor(model, levels = c("Random effect", "Interaction"))
  )

cohort_plot <- cohort_tests |>
  mutate(cohort = factor(cohort, levels = names(cohort_colours)))

ggplot() +
  geom_density(
    data = draws_plot,
    aes(x = baseline_log_mu, fill = model),
    colour = NA,
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    data = cohort_plot,

    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = model_colours) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = cohort_colours) +
  facet_wrap(~ gene, scales = "free", ncol = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Revised healthy liver NK baseline by family, with HCC cohorts",
    subtitle = "Filled densities = simple-shape baseline log(mu) per family; lines = edgeR cohort log(mu) at offset 0",
    x = "log(mu)",
    y = "Density",
    fill = "Baseline family",
    colour = "HCC cohort"
  ) +

    legend.position = "bottom",

Which baseline serves the case study?

The case study expects recurrent (REC) cohorts to sit farther from the healthy liver NK reference than non-recurrent (non-REC) cohorts. We quantify each cohort’s distance from each baseline as a standardized deviation z = (cohort log(μ) − baseline mean log(μ)) / baseline SD, then compare the absolute distance of REC vs non-REC within each gene x compartment. We do this for all four baseline variants (family x shape) so the shape effect on case-study discrimination is visible too — a narrower baseline should give larger standardized separation.

Code 
baseline_stats <- draws_df |>
  mutate(
    model = recode(model, !!!model_labels),
    shape = recode(shape_variant, !!!shape_labels)
  ) |>
  group_by(gene, model, shape) |>
  summarise(
    baseline_mean_log_mu = mean(baseline_log_mu),
    baseline_sd_log_mu = sd(baseline_log_mu),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

cohort_projection <- cohort_tests |>
  inner_join(baseline_stats, by = "gene", relationship = "many-to-many") |>
  mutate(
    signed_z = (cohort_log_mu - baseline_mean_log_mu) / baseline_sd_log_mu,
    abs_z = abs(signed_z)
  )

cohort_projection |>
  filter(shape == "Simple shape (revised)") |>
  select(
    gene, model, cohort, cohort_log_mu, baseline_mean_log_mu,
    baseline_sd_log_mu, signed_z, abs_z
  ) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3))) |>
  arrange(gene, model, cohort)
Code 
recurrence_margin <- cohort_projection |>
  select(gene, compartment, recurrence, model, shape, abs_z) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = recurrence, values_from = abs_z) |>
  mutate(
    margin_rec_minus_nonrec = REC - `non-REC`,
    rec_farther_from_healthy = margin_rec_minus_nonrec > 0
  )

recurrence_margin |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3))) |>
  arrange(gene, compartment, model, shape)

A positive margin_rec_minus_nonrec means the REC cohort is farther from the healthy baseline than the non-REC cohort — the direction the HCC case study predicts. Summarising across all gene x compartment comparisons:

Code 
baseline_choice <- recurrence_margin |>
  group_by(model, shape) |>
  summarise(
    n_comparisons = n(),
    n_rec_farther = sum(rec_farther_from_healthy),
    frac_rec_farther = mean(rec_farther_from_healthy),
    mean_margin_sd = mean(margin_rec_minus_nonrec),
    median_margin_sd = median(margin_rec_minus_nonrec),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(n_rec_farther), desc(mean_margin_sd))

baseline_choice
Code 
baseline_choice |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = c("Random effect", "Interaction"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = model, y = mean_margin_sd, fill = shape)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.7), width = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    `Rich shape (reference)` = "#E64B35",
    `Simple shape (revised)` = "#4DBBD5"
  )) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Mean REC - non-REC separation (baseline SD units)",
    fill = NULL,
    title = "Case-study discrimination by baseline variant",
    subtitle = "Higher = recurrent cohorts sit farther from healthy, as expected"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
Code 
best <- baseline_choice |> slice(1)
re_simple <- baseline_choice |>
  filter(model == "Random effect", shape == "Simple shape (revised)")
int_simple <- baseline_choice |>
  filter(model == "Interaction", shape == "Simple shape (revised)")

cat(glue(
  "Among the revised (simple-shape) candidates, the ",
  "**{re_simple$model}** baseline recovers the expected ",
  "REC-farther-from-healthy ordering in ",
  "{re_simple$n_rec_farther}/{re_simple$n_comparisons} cases (mean separation ",
  "{round(re_simple$mean_margin_sd, 2)} SD), versus ",
  "{int_simple$n_rec_farther}/{int_simple$n_comparisons} and ",
  "{round(int_simple$mean_margin_sd, 2)} SD for the {int_simple$model} baseline. ",
  "Across all four variants, the best case-study discrimination comes from the ",
  "**{best$model} / {best$shape}** baseline. "
))

Among the revised (simple-shape) candidates, the Random effect baseline recovers the expected REC-farther-from-healthy ordering in 8/8 cases (mean separation 1.19 SD), versus 8/8 and 0.57 SD for the Interaction baseline. Across all four variants, the best case-study discrimination comes from the Random effect / Rich shape (reference) baseline.

Reading this together with the shape result. Because the cohort projections are fixed, the standardized REC vs non-REC separation scales inversely with the baseline SD. So whichever variant most tightens the baseline (see the shape section above) also delivers the cleanest case-study discrimination. If the simple shape narrows the baseline as hypothesised, the revised baselines should push recurrent cohorts farther outside the healthy envelope than the rich reference — exactly the behaviour the HCC proximity score relies on. The partial-pooling random-effect family remains the more conservative, better-identified liver reference at liver n = 71.

Interpretation

Code 
n_genes <- dplyr::n_distinct(baseline_summary$gene)
n_narrower <- sum(shape_effect$sd_ratio_simple_over_rich < 1, na.rm = TRUE)
n_total <- sum(is.finite(shape_effect$sd_ratio_simple_over_rich))
mean_ratio <- mean(shape_effect$sd_ratio_simple_over_rich, na.rm = TRUE)
mean_shift <- mean(abs(shape_effect$mean_shift_simple_minus_rich), na.rm = TRUE)

cat(glue(
  "Across {n_genes} genes and both families, simplifying the shape formula ",
  "narrows the liver baseline in {n_narrower}/{n_total} cells ",
  "(mean SD ratio {round(mean_ratio, 2)}), while shifting the baseline mean by ",
  "only {round(mean_shift, 2)} log units on average. ",
  if (n_narrower > n_total / 2 && mean_ratio < 1) {
    "This is consistent with the shape (dispersion) formula — not the mean formula — being the dominant driver of baseline uncertainty: letting dispersion pool across tissues tightens the posterior without moving the mean."
  } else {
    "The shape formula is therefore not the dominant driver of baseline uncertainty here."
  }
))

Across 4 genes and both families, simplifying the shape formula narrows the liver baseline in 3/8 cells (mean SD ratio 0.99), while shifting the baseline mean by only 0.25 log units on average. The shape formula is therefore not the dominant driver of baseline uncertainty here.

Shape (dispersion) formula. The revised simple shape drops the ethnicity/tissue-specific dispersion terms so the negative-binomial shape is estimated by pooling across all tissues instead of leaning on the 71 liver rows. The SD-by-shape comparison isolates this effect while holding each family’s mean formula fixed.

Random-effect family. Liver tissue intercepts and slopes are partially pooled toward a blood-informed population mean. This reduces variance but can bias liver estimates toward the dominant tissue when liver-specific signal is weak. The rich-shape RE reference is the well-converged production fit.

Interaction family. Liver is estimated without mean-model shrinkage but at the cost of many tissue × covariate coefficients; with 21 tissues and sparse liver covariate combinations the fits can be unstable (wide baselines, divergences), and a rich shape compounds this.

Implication for HCC. A tighter, better-identified liver baseline directly sharpens the healthy-proximity score, because the standardized REC vs non-REC separation scales inversely with baseline SD. If the simple shape is confirmed to control the SD, the revised baselines are preferable for the case study; choosing between the two families is then a bias/variance trade-off to settle in downstream HCC ranking tests.
